{{Short description|Polynomial root-finding algorithm}}
{{about|the [[root-finding algorithm]]|an unrelated topic in [[ordinary differential equation]]|Bernoulli differential equation| an unrelated topic in [[fluid dynamics]]|Bernoulli's principle}}

[[File:Excerpt from Observationes de Seriebvs.png|thumb|Excerpt from Observations Concerning Series by [[Daniel Bernoulli]] published in 1729.<ref name="excerpt">{{cite journal |last1=Bernoulli |first1=Daniel |title=Observations de Seriebus |date=1729 |journal=Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae |volume=t.3 |pages=92 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/38524#page/7/mode/1up |publisher=Typis Academiae}}</ref>]]

In [[numerical analysis]], '''Bernoulli's method''', named after [[Daniel Bernoulli]], is a [[root-finding algorithm]] which calculates the [[polynomial|root]] of largest [[absolute value]] of a [[univariate polynomial]].<ref name="henrici">{{cite book |last1=Henrici |first1=Peter |title=Elements Of Numerical Analysis |date=1965 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |url=https://archive.org/details/elements-of-numerical-analysis-by-peter-henrici |pages=146–179}}</ref><ref name="pan">{{cite book |last1=McNamee |first1=J. M. |last2=Pan |first2=V. Y. |title=Studies in Computational Mathematics |date=1 January 2013 |publisher=Elsevier |pages=381–460 |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-444-52730-1.00004-7 |chapter=Chapter 10 - Bernoulli, Quotient-Difference, and Integral Methods|volume=16 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-444-52730-1.00004-7 |isbn=978-0-444-52730-1 |url-access=limited}}</ref> The method works under the condition that there is only one root (possibly multiple) of  maximal absolute value. The method computes the root of maximal absolute value as the [[limit (mathematics)|limit]] of the [[quotient]]s of two successive terms of a [[sequence]] defined by a [[linear recurrence]] whose coefficients are those of  the polynomial.

Since the method converges with a [[Rate of convergence|linear order]] only, it is less efficient than other methods, such as [[Newton's method]]. However, it can be useful for finding an initial guess ensuring that these other methods converge to the root of maximal absolute value.<ref name="jennings">{{cite book |last1=Jennings |first1=Walter |title=First course in numerical methods |date=1964 |publisher=Macmillan |location=New York |page=31 |url=https://archive.org/details/firstcourseinnum0000jenn/page/31/mode/1up |url-access=registration}}</ref> Bernoulli's method holds [[historical significance]] as an early approach to numerical root-finding and provides an elegant connection between [[Recurrence relation|recurrence relations]] and polynomial roots.

== History ==
[[File:Lagrange on Bernoulli's method.png|thumb|[[Joseph-Louis Lagrange|Lagrange]] on Bernoulli's method.<ref name="lagrange">{{cite book |last1=Lagrange |first1=Joseph-Louis |title=Traité de la résolution des équations numériques de tous les degrés , avec des notes sur plusieurs points de la théorie des équations algébriques ; par J.-L. Lagrange, de l'Institut des sciences... Nouvelle édition, revue et augmentée par l'auteur |date=1808 |page=136 |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k1042793z |language=FR |chapter=Note VI}}</ref>]]
Bernoulli's method was first introduced by [[Switzerland|Swiss]]-[[France|French]] [[mathematician]] and [[physicist]] [[Daniel Bernoulli]] (1700-1782) in 1728.<ref name="excerpt" /><ref name="chabert">{{cite book |editor1-last=Chabert |editor1-first=Jean-Luc |title=A history of algorithms : from the pebble to the microchip |date=1999 |location=Berlin; New York |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-63369-3 |pages=223–224 |url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_0116404090940/page/222/mode/2up}}</ref> He noticed a trend from recurrent series created using polynomial coefficients growing by a ratio related to a root of the polynomial but did not prove why it worked.<ref name="chabert" /> In 1725, Bernoulli moved to [[Saint Petersburg]] with his brother [[Nicolaus II Bernoulli]], who unfortunately died of fever in 1726.<ref name="mathshistory">{{cite web |last1=O'Connor |first1=J J |last2=Robertson |first2=E F |title=Daniel Bernoulli - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Bernoulli_Daniel/ |website=Maths History |publisher=University of St. Andrews |language=en}}</ref> While there, he worked closely with [[Leonhard Euler]], a student of [[Johann Bernoulli]], and made many advancements in [[harmonics]], [[mathematical economics]] (see [[St. Petersburg paradox]]), and [[hydrodynamics]].<ref name="mathshistory" /> Euler called Bernoulli's method "frequently very useful" and gave a justification for why it works in 1748.<ref name="euler">{{cite book |last1=Euler |title=Introduction to Analysis of the Infinite: Book I |date=1988 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-4612-1021-4 |pages=283–302 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4612-1021-4_17 |chapter-url-access=limited |language=en |chapter=Using Recurrent Series to Find Roots of Equations|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-1021-4_17 }}</ref><ref name="pan" /> The mathematician [[Joseph-Louis Lagrange]] expanded on this for the case of multiple roots in 1798.<ref name="lagrange" /><ref name="pan" /> Bernoulli's method predates other root-finding algorithms like [[Graeffe's method]] (1826 to Dandelin)<ref name="dandelin">{{cite journal |last1=Dandelin |first1=G. |title=Recherches sur la résolution des équations numériques. |journal=Nouveaux mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences et Belles-Lettres de Bruxelles |date=1826 |volume=3 |pages=7–37 |url=https://eudml.org/doc/180464}}</ref><ref name="householder">{{cite journal |last1=Householder |first1=Alston S. |title=Dandelin, Lobacevskii, or Graeffe |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |date=1959 |volume=66 |issue=6 |pages=464–466 |doi=10.2307/2310626 |jstor=2310626 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2310626 |url-access=limited |issn=0002-9890}}</ref> and is contemporary to [[Halley's method]] (1694).<ref name="halley">{{cite journal |last1=Halley |first1=Edmond |title=Methodus nova accurata & facilis inveniendi radices æqnationum quarumcumque generaliter, sine praviæ reductione |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London |date=May 1694 |volume=18 |issue=210 |pages=136–148 |doi=10.1098/rstl.1694.0029 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="scavo">{{cite journal |last1=Scavo |first1=T. R. |last2=Thoo |first2=J. B. |title=On the Geometry of Halley's Method |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00029890.1995.12004594 |url-access=limited |date=May 1995 |volume=102 |issue=5 |pages=417–426 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1995.12004594}}</ref> Since then, it has influenced the development of more modern algorithms such as the QD method.<ref name="rutishauser1">{{cite journal |last1=Rutishauser |first1=Heinz |title=Der Quotienten-Differenzen-Algorithmus |journal=Zeitschrift für angewandte Mathematik und Physik |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01600331 |date=May 1954 |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=233–251 |url-access=limited |doi=10.1007/BF01600331|bibcode=1954ZaMP....5..233R }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Henrici |first1=Peter |chapter=Topics in Computational Complex Analysis: II. New Developments Concerning the Quotient-Difference Algorithm |title=Computational Aspects of Complex Analysis |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-94-009-7121-9_6 |chapter-url-access=limited |date=1983 |pages=149–168 |doi=10.1007/978-94-009-7121-9_6|isbn=978-94-009-7123-3 }}</ref>

== The method ==
Given a polynomial 
<math display=block> p = a_{0}z^d + a_{1}z^{d-1} + \dots + a_d </math> 
of degree {{mvar|d}} with [[Complex number|complex coefficients]]. Choose {{mvar|d}} starting values <math>x_{-d+1}, x_{-d}, \dots, x_{-1}, x_0,</math> that are usually <math>0, 0, 0, \dots, 0, 1</math>.<ref name="blum">{{cite book |last1=Blum |first1=E. K. (Edward K. ) |title=Numerical analysis and computation theory and practice |date=1972 |publisher=Reading, Mass., Addison-Wesley Pub. Co |url=https://archive.org/details/numericalanalysi0000blum/page/n3/mode/2up |pages=210–211 |url-access=registration}}</ref> Then, consider the sequence defined by the [[recurrence relation]]<ref name="henrici" />
<math display=block> x_n = -\frac{a_1 x_{n-1} + a_2 x_{n-2} + \dots + a_d x_{n-d}}{a_0} .</math>

Let <math display=inline>q_n = \frac{x_{n+1}}{x_n}</math> be the ratio of successive terms of the sequence. If there is only one complex root of maximal absolute value, then the sequence of the {{tmath|q_n}} has a limit that is this root.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Weisstein |first1=Eric W. |title=Bernoulli's Method |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/BernoullisMethod.html |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref> 

If the coefficients of the polynomial are real then, via the [[complex conjugate root theorem]], each of the polynomial's roots must be either a [[real number]] or part of a [[complex conjugate]] pair. Therefore, if the polynomial contains a single dominant complex root, then the coefficients must include a [[complex number]], and so the sequence generated using the coefficients will contain complex numbers. Bernoulli's method will work to find a single dominant root, regardless of whether it is real or complex.<ref name="henrici" /> If a root is part of a [[complex conjugate]] pair, then each root in the pair has the same maximal absolute value, and a modified form of Bernoulli's method is needed to calculate them.<ref name="pan" />

== Derivation of the method ==

The solutions of the <math>n-</math>th order [[difference equation]]
:<math> a_n x_m + a_{n-1} x_{m-1} + \dots + a_0 x_{m-n} = 0</math>
have the form  
:<math> x_m = c_1(m)r_1^m + c_2(m) r_2^m + \dots + c_k(m) r_k^m ,</math>
where the <math>r_i</math> are the distinct complex  roots of <math>p(z)</math>, and <math>c_i(m)</math> is polynomial in <math>m</math> of degree less than the multiplicity of <math>r_i</math>. For simple roots, <math>c_i</math> is a constant. The coefficients <math>c_i</math> can be determined from the first <math>n</math> terms of the sequence <math>x_m</math> by solving a linear system of equations. This system has always a unique solution since its matrix is a [[Vandermonde matrix]] if the roots are simple, or a [[Vandermonde matrix#Confluent Vandermonde matrices|confluent Vandermonde matrix]] otherwise.<ref name="whittaker">{{cite book |last1=Whittaker |first1=E. T. |url=https://archive.org/details/calculusofobserv031400mbp |title=The Calculus Of Observations |last2=Robinson |first2=G. |date=1924 |publisher=Blackie and Son |pages=98–99 |chapter=52. The Method of Daniel Bernoulli.}}</ref> 

The quotient of two successive terms of the sequence is
:<math> \frac{x_{m+1}}{x_m} = \frac{c_1(m+1) r_1^{m+1} + c_2(m+1) r_2^{m+1} + \dots + c_k(m+1) r_k^{m+1}}
{c_1(m) r_1^m + c_2(m) r_2^m + \dots + c_k(m) r_k^m}. </math>

Factoring out <math>r_1</math> gives
:<math> \frac{x_{m+1}}{x_m} = r_1 \cdot \frac{c_1(m+1) + c_2(m+1) \left( \frac{r_2}{r_1} \right)^{m+1} + \dots + c_k(m+1) \left( \frac{r_k}{r_1} \right)^{m+1}}
{c_1(m) + c_2(m) \left( \frac{r_2}{r_1} \right)^m + \dots + c_k(m) \left( \frac{r_k}{r_1} \right)^m} .</math>

Assuming <math>r_1</math> is the dominant root, such that <math>|r_1| > |r_i|</math> for {{tmath|i>1}}, each ratio <math display=inline>\frac{r_i}{r_1}</math> has an absolute value less than 1. Thus as {{mvar|m}} increases, <math display=inline>\left( \frac{r_i}{r_1} \right)^m</math> approaches zero, so <math display=inline>\lim_{m \to \infty} c_i(m)\left( \frac{r_i}{r_1} \right)^m = 0,</math> even for non-constant <math display=inline>c_i(m)</math>. Hence the limit of the fraction is the same as that of <math display=inline>\frac{c_1(m+1)}{c_1(m)},</math> which is 1 if {{tmath|c_i}} is a constant or a nonzero polynomial in {{mvar|m}}.

Hence <math display=block>\lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{x_{m+1}}{x_m} = r_1</math>
in all cases where there is only one root of maximal absolute value.<ref name="encyc">{{cite web |title=Bernoulli method |url=https://encyclopediaofmath.org/wiki/Bernoulli_method |website=encyclopediaofmath.org |publisher=Encyclopedia of Mathematics |access-date=20 April 2025}}</ref> 

This assumes <math>c_1 \neq 0,</math> which is satisfied by using initial values of all zeros followed by a final 1.<ref name="blum" /> Indeed, [[Cramer's rule]] implies that <math>c_1</math> is a signed quotient of two nonsingular Vandermonde matrices, if all roots are simple; in the case of multiple roots, the dominant coefficient of <math>c_1(m)</math> is a signed quotient of two nonsingular confluent matrices.

== Extensions ==
[[File:Aitken-excerpt.png|thumb|Excerpt by [[Alexander Aitken|Aitken]] on his extension of Bernoulli's method.<ref name="aitken" />]]
Bernoulli's method converges to the root of largest modulus of a polynomial with a linear [[order of convergence]].<ref name="pan" /> It does not converge when there are two distinct complex roots of the same largest modulus, but there are extensions of the method that work in this case.<ref name="henrici" /> For finding the root of smallest absolute value, one can apply the method on the [[reciprocal polynomial]] (polynomial obtained by reversing the order of the coefficients), and inverting the result. When using [[Ruffini's rule|root deflation]] with something like [[Horner's method]], deflating from the smallest root is more [[Numerical stability|stable]].<ref name="wilkinson">{{cite book |last1=Wilkinson |first1=J. H. (James Hardy) |title=Rounding errors in algebraic processes |date=1963 |location=Englewood Cliffs, N.J. |publisher=Prentice-Hall |pages=59–62 |url=https://archive.org/details/roundingerrorsin0000wilk}}</ref>

To speed convergence, [[Alexander Aitken]] developed his [[Aitken delta-squared process]] as part of an improvement on his extension to Bernoulli's method, which also found all of the roots simultaneously.<ref name="aitken">{{cite journal |last1=Aitken |first1=A. C. |title=XXV.—On Bernoulli's Numerical Solution of Algebraic Equations |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-royal-society-of-edinburgh/article/abs/xxvon-bernoullis-numerical-solution-of-algebraic-equations/64D4A7C56F1EFEC696AF68D7870DB451 |url-access=limited |date=January 1927 |volume=46 |pages=289–305 |doi=10.1017/S0370164600022070}}</ref><ref name="genesis-aitken">{{cite journal |last1=Brezinski |first1=Claude |last2=Redivo–Zaglia |first2=Michela |title=The genesis and early developments of Aitken's process, Shanks' transformation, the ε–algorithm, and related fixed point methods |journal=Numerical Algorithms |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11075-018-0567-2 |url-access=limited |date=January 2019 |volume=80 |issue=1 |pages=11–133 |doi=10.1007/s11075-018-0567-2}}</ref> Another extension of Bernoulli's method is the Quotient-Difference (QD) method, which also finds all roots simultaneously, even though it can be unstable.<ref name="pan" /> Given the slow convergence of Bernoulli's method, and the instability of QD method, they can instead be used as reliable ways to find starting values for other root-finding algorithms, rather than iterated until tolerance.<ref name="henrici2">{{cite journal |last1=Henrici |first1=P. |last2=Watkins |first2=Bruce O. |title=Finding zeros of a polynomial by the Q-D algorithm |journal=Communications of the ACM |date=September 1965 |volume=8 |issue=9 |pages=570–574 |doi=10.1145/365559.365619 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Example ==
[[File:X^2-x-1.svg|thumb|Plot of the example polynomial on a [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian plane]] showing the dominant root at <math display=inline>\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}, 0\right)</math>.]]
[[File:Bernoulli Method Convergence Example.svg|thumb|Bernoulli's method convergence on the root of <math>p(z)=z^2-z-1</math>.]]
The following example illustrates Bernoulli's method applied to a quadratic polynomial. Let <math display=inline>p(z) = z^2 - z - 1 = 0</math>. Then <math>a_0 = 1</math>, <math>a_1 = -1</math>, and <math>a_2 = -1</math>, so the recurrence becomes:
 
<math>
\begin{align}
x_n &= -\frac{(-1)x_{n-1} + (-1)x_{n-2}}{1}\\
    &= x_{n-1} + x_{n-2}
\end{align}
</math>

Using the recommended initial values <math>x_{-1} = 0</math>, <math>x_0 = 1</math> generates the following table:

{| class=wikitable style="border: none;"
! scope=col | {{math|''n''}}
! scope=col | {{math|''x''<sub>''n''</sub>}}
! scope=col | {{math|''q''<sub>''n''</sub>}}
! scope=col | {{math|&#124;''q''<sub>''n''</sub> - φ&#124;}}
! scope=col | {{math|order}}
|-
| -1 || 0 || − || − || −
|-
| 0 || 1 || 1 || 0.618033989 || −
|-
| 1 || 1 || 2 || 0.381966011 || 2.44042009
|-
| 2 || 2 || 1.5 || 0.118033989 || 0.766784227
|- 
| 3 || 3 || 1.666 || 0.047966011 || 1.086347793
|-
| 4 || 5 || 1.6 || 0.018033989 || 0.972379866
|-
| 5 || 8 || 1.625 || 0.006966011 || 1.016299341
|-
| 6 || 13 || 1.61538461538 || 0.002649373 || 0.993860956
|-
| 7 || 21 || 1.61904761905 || 0.00101363 || 1.002357448
|-
| 8 || 34 || 1.61764705882 || 0.00038693 || 0.999101399
|-
| 9 || 55 || 1.61818181818 || 0.000147829 || 1.000343479
|}

This eventually converges on <math display=inline>\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 1.618034</math>, also known as the [[Golden ratio]], which is the largest root of the example polynomial. The sequence <math>{x_n}</math> is also the well-known [[Fibonacci sequence]]. Bernoulli's method works even if the sequence used different starting values instead of 0 and 1; the limit of the quotient <math>q_n</math> remains the same.

The example also shows the [[Approximation error|absolute error]] approaching zero as the sequence continues. It is then possible to calculate the [[Rate of convergence|order of convergence]] using three contiguous errors. This example demonstrates that Bernoulli's method converged linearly as it approaches the dominant root of the polynomial.

== Comparison with other methods ==
Compared to other root-finding algorithms, Bernoulli's method offers distinct advantages and limitations. The following table summarizes several important differences of Bernoulli's method in comparison with other methods:

! Convergence Order
! Initial Guess
! Multiple Roots
! Uses Derivatives

|}

=== Advantages ===
* No initial guess: [[Newton's method]], [[Secant method]], [[Halley's method]], and other similar approaches, all require one or more starting values.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Qureshi |first1=Sania |last2=Soomro |first2=Amanullah |last3=Naseem |first3=Amir |last4=Gdawiec |first4=Krzysztof |last5=Argyros |first5=Ioannis K. |last6=Alshaery |first6=Aisha A. |last7=Secer |first7=Aydin |title=From Halley to Secant: Redefining root finding with memory-based methods including convergence and stability |journal=Mathematical Methods in the Applied Sciences |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mma.9876 |url-access=limited |date=15 May 2024 |volume=47 |issue=7 |pages=5509–5531 |doi=10.1002/mma.9876|bibcode=2024MMAS...47.5509Q }}</ref> Bernoulli's method requires only the polynomial coefficients, eliminating the need for an initial guess.
* No derivatives: Although derivatives of polynomials are straightforward with the [[power rule]], this is a computation that is not required in Bernoulli's method.
* Naturally finds a dominant root: Normally, finding large roots is considered less stable, but substituting {{mvar|z}} in {{mvar|p}} with <math display=inline>\left(\frac{1}{z}\right)</math>, which reverses the order of coefficients, and then inverting the result of Bernoulli's method gives the smallest root of {{mvar|p}}, which is more stable.<ref name="euler" /><ref name="wilkinson" />

=== Limitations ===

* Slow convergence: Fröberg writes "As a rule, Bernoulli's method converges slowly, so instead, one ought to use, for example, the Newton-Raphson method."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Fröberg |first1=Carl Erik |title=Introduction to numerical analysis |date=1965 |location=Reading, Mass. |publisher=Addison-Wesley |pages=232–233 |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontonu0000frob_u5p6/page/232/mode/2up |url-access=registration}}</ref> This is in contrast to Jennings, who writes "The approximate zeros obtained by the Bernoulli method can be further improved by applying, say, the Newton-Raphson method".<ref name="jennings" /> One author argues for instead-of while the other promotes in-conjunction-with, due to the linear order of convergence. The slow convergence can be improved with [[Aitken's delta-squared process]].<ref name="aitken" />
* Finds one root at a time: The standard version of Bernoulli's method finds a single root, requiring deflation to find another. When compared to algorithms such as [[Durand–Kerner method]], [[Aberth method]], [[Bairstow's method]], and the "RPOLY" version of [[Jenkins–Traub algorithm]] they find multiple roots by default. One can overcome this limitation by applying an extension of Bernoulli's method such as the method by Aitken or QD method.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Henrici |first1=Peter |title=The quotient-difference algorithm |journal=Applied Mathematics Series |date=1958 |volume=49 |pages=23–46 |url=https://hdl.handle.net/2027/uiug.30112007252650?urlappend=%3Bseq=441 |publisher=U.S. Dept. of Commerce, National Bureau of Standards |hdl=2027/uiug.30112007252650?urlappend=%3Bseq=441 |hdl-access=free |language=en}}</ref>
* Issues with multiples: Multiplicity and multiple dominant roots, such as conjugate pairs, can exacerbate the slowness of Bernoulli's method, yet improvements can be made to counter this.<ref name="dimsdale">{{cite journal |last1=Dimsdale |first1=Bernard |title=On Bernoulli's Method for Solving Algebraic Equations |journal=Quarterly of Applied Mathematics |date=1948 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=77–81 |doi=10.1090/qam/24237 |jstor=43633641 |issn=0033-569X |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="dimsdale2">{{cite book |last1=Dimsdale |first1=Bernard |title=Proceedings of the 1956 11th ACM national meeting on - ACM '56 |chapter=On Bernoulli's method for solving algebraic equations, II |date=1956 |pages=21–24 |doi=10.1145/800258.808939 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Modern applications ==
[[File:EDSAC_(19).jpg|thumb|The Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator ([[EDSAC]]) at the University of Cambridge Mathematical Laboratory in England, 1948]]
Bernoulli's method, despite its linear convergence, remains relevant in computational mathematics with finding initial values for [[Polynomial root-finding]] algorithms and extensions to more general mathematical domains.<ref name="jennings" /> It can also be used to find complex roots<ref name="henrici" /> yet the more sophisticated extensions of Bernoulli's method, such as the one by Aitken<ref name="aitken" /> and QD method,<ref name="henrici" /> are able to find complex roots while solving for all of the roots simultaneously. There are also variations on Bernoulli's method that improve stability and handle multiple roots.<ref name="dimsdale" /><ref name="dimsdale2" /> A 2025 analysis of the QD method included an implementation in [[C (programming language)|C]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Debnath |first1=G. |last2=Vasu |first2=B. |title=Quotient-Difference Algorithm and Code for Cubic Polynomials with Computational Implementation |journal=Numerical Analysis and Applications |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S1995423924600093 |url-access=limited |date=March 2025 |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=44–58 |doi=10.1134/s1995423924600093}}</ref>

In related applications, Bernoulli's method has been shown to be equivalent to [[Power method]] on a [[companion matrix]] for finding [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]].<ref name="young">{{cite book |last1=Young |first1=David M. |title=A survey of numerical mathematics |date=1972 |location=Reading, Mass. |publisher=Addison-Wesley |pages=219–220 |url=https://archive.org/details/surveyofnumerica0001youn/mode/1up |url-access=registration}}</ref> Advancements in [[systolic array]]s have led to a parallelized version of Bernoulli's method.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Margaritis |first1=K |last2=Evans |first2=D.J |title=Systolic designs for Bernoulli's method |journal=Parallel Computing |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/016781919090045B |url-access=limited |date=September 1990 |volume=15 |issue=1–3 |pages=227–240 |doi=10.1016/0167-8191(90)90045-B}}</ref> The method has also been generalized to find [[zeros and poles|poles]] of [[Rational function|rational functions]], extending to the field of [[complex analysis]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dózsa |first1=Tamás |last2=Schipp |first2=Ferenc |last3=Soumelidis |first3=Alexandros |title=On Bernoulli's Method |journal=SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis |date=30 June 2024 |volume=62 |issue=3 |pages=1259–1277 |doi=10.1137/22M1528501|url=https://eprints.sztaki.hu/10733/ |doi-access=free}}</ref> An extension of Bernoulli's method was used for improving [[Linear multistep method|linear multistep methods]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kireev |first1=I. V. |last2=Novikov |first2=A. E. |last3=Novikov |first3=E. A. |title=Stability Domains of Explicit Multistep Methods |journal=Numerical Analysis and Applications |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S1995423922040073 |url-access=limited |date=December 2022 |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=343–352 |doi=10.1134/S1995423922040073}}</ref> Another development of a modified Bernoulli's method builds a supplemental function using [[Taylor series|Taylor]] and [[Laurent series|Laurent]] series expansions to then solve for roots.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lebedev |first1=A. V. |last2=Trubnikov |first2=Yu. V. |last3=Chernyavsky |first3=M. M. |title=On the Bernoulli–Euler–Lagrange–Aitken numerical method for roots of polynomials |journal=Doklady of the National Academy of Sciences of Belarus |date=30 October 2023 |volume=67 |issue=5 |pages=359–365 |doi=10.29235/1561-8323-2023-67-359-365|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lebedev |first1=A. V. |last2=Trubnikov |first2=Yu. V. |last3=Chernyavsky |first3=M. M. |title=On the Hadamard and Vandermonde Determinants and the Bernoulli–Euler–Lagrange–Aitken Method for Calculating the Roots of Polynomials |journal=Mathematical Notes |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1134/S0001434624070071 |url-access=limited |date=August 2024 |volume=116 |issue=1–2 |pages=77–92 |doi=10.1134/S0001434624070071}}</ref> An implementation of Bernoulli's method is included with the CodeCogs [[open source]] numerical methods library.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bentea |first1=Lucian |title=Bernoulli - Rootfinding - Maths in C, C++ |url=https://www.codecogs.com/library/maths/rootfinding/bernoulli.php |website=www.codecogs.com}}</ref> The method was also programmed on the [[EDSAC]], along with [[Graeffe's method]], but [[Newton's method]] was preferred for being faster.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brooker |first1=R. A. |title=The solution of algebraic equations on the EDSAC |journal=[[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]] |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-proceedings-of-the-cambridge-philosophical-society/article/abs/solution-of-algebraic-equations-on-the-edsac/01E6A530985EBAE6848CCB5958258649 |url-access=limited |date=April 1952 |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=255–270 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100027614|bibcode=1952PCPS...48..255B }}</ref>

== Code ==
Bernoulli's method is implemented below in the [[Python (programming language)|Python]] programming language. 

<syntaxhighlight lang="python3">
def bernoulli_method(c, eps=1e-8, max_iter=60):
    """
    Bernoulli's method for finding the dominant root of a polynomial.

    Parameters
    ----------
    c : list
        List of polynomial coefficients in descending order of powers.
        For example, if p(x) = x^2 - x - 1, c = [1.0, -1.0, -1.0]
    eps : float, optional
        Convergence tolerance. Default is 1e-8.
    max_iter : int, optional
        Maximum number of iterations. Default is 60.

    Returns
    -------
    float or complex
        The dominant root of the polynomial if found, otherwise float('nan').

    Examples
    --------
    >>> bernoulli_method([1.0, -1.0, -1.0])  # Golden ratio example
    1.6180339901755971
    >>> bernoulli_method([1.0, -3.0, 2.0])   # x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 2)(x - 1)
    2.0000000074505806
    """
    n = len(c)
    x = [0.0] * (n - 2) + [1.0]  # Initialize with zeros and a 1.0
    q = []

    for i in range(n - 1, max_iter + n):
        # Apply the recurrence relation: x_n = -(a_1*x_{n-1} + ... + a_d*x_{n-d})/a_0
        x.append(-sum(c[k] * x[-k + i] for k in range(1, n)) / c[0])
        q.append(x[-1] / x[-2])  # Quotient of two successive x terms q_n = x_{n+1} / x_n

        # Check for convergence after two quotient values
        if len(q) >= 2 and abs(q[-1] - q[-2]) <= eps:
            return q[-1]  # Return the last computed quotient

    return float("nan")  # No convergence within max_iter
</syntaxhighlight>

An efficiency improvement would be to normalize the coefficients by the leading coefficient at the beginning of the method (<code>c = [coef / c[0] for coef in c]</code>), eliminating the need for a division operation in the recurrence relation inside the main loop body (<code>x.append(-sum(c[k] * x[-k + i] for k in range(1, n)))</code>). This change does not impact the convergence order of the method. Implementing higher-order convergence would require [[Aitken's delta-squared process]].
